newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian budget seen boosting finance sector.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian budget seen boosting finance sector.

text.p: Malaysia's 1997 national budget is aimed at nurturing the financial sector and jump-starting an information technology industry as the basis for future growth, officials and analysts said at the weekend.

On Friday Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim unveiled a 59.98 billion ringgit ($23.9 billion) budget -- 1.2 percent lower than last year's -- that is mildy contractionary in an economy well into its ninth straight year of eight-plus percent growth.
Until now, growth has been driven by an export-oriented manufacturing base, built largely by billions of dollars in foreign investment.
But in his speech to parliament Anwar said reliance on foreign capital for growth had to be reduced if Malaysia was to maintain its competitive edge in the global economy.

"Our economy must be driven by intellectual and creative energy," said Anwar, who is also deputy prime minister. "The manufacturing sector will continue to be important but the new stimulus will come from services and information-based industries."
In a budget that even Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad described as "not that exciting", Anwar's budget focused on measures to boost the financial services industry. Among them:
-- Foreign fund managers can take up to a 49 percent equity stake in local brokerages;
-- Broking firms are permitted to set up unit trusts, undertake fund management and underwriting, issue call warrants and manage the listing of companies;
-- A zero-coupon bond will be introduced to provide a benchmark yield curve to stimulate the moribund debt market;
-- Private firms will be allowed to issue ringgit-denominated bonds;
-- An over-the-counter (OTC) market will be established to trade shares in new high-technology companies;
-- Additional tax breaks will be given to firms and foreign workers in the Labuan Island offshore financial centre.
Pacific Bank Bhd chairman Lin See Yan, a former central bank deputy governor, said he was particularly impressed with the benchmark bond announcement.

"Without a benchmark bond it will be difficult to develop the secondary market," he told reporters. "Even though no details are given at this juncture, the fact that the finance minister is tackling the basic problem ... is encouraging."

The Ratings Association of Malaysia, one of two independent agencies that rate securities in the country said: "We see (the benchmark bond) as the right move to activate the secondary bond market by providing the risk-free yield curve for issuers, arrangers and investors to avoid mispricing."

Amirsham Aziz, chairman of the Association of Banks Malaysia, said the various measures for the industry "would not only support the growth of the economy but also position Malaysia as a user-friendly financial centre and significant global player".
The other major initiative in the budget was a package of incentives for a multimedia zone that Malaysia is establishing to attract information technology firms.

Anwar said pioneer companies that moved to the zone -- which extends south from Kuala Lumpur to where a new airport and federal capital are under construction -- would be given 10-year tax exemptions.
There would be tax exemptions on multimedia equipment and relaxed procedures for hiring expatriate workers, he added.
